content.title: About
content.content: Quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa) is a seed from the Andes of South America that is cooked and eaten like a grain, although it is not a true cereal. The tiny round seeds come in white, red, and black varieties and have a mild, nutty flavor and a fluffy texture with a slight pop. Quinoa is naturally gluten-free and used in salads, bowls, soups, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quinoa has been grown in the Andes for thousands of years and was a sacred crop of the Inca.
It is a pseudocereal related to beets, spinach, and chard, not to wheat or rice.
Quinoa is a complete protein, containing all nine essential amino acids.
Quinoa seeds are coated with natural bitter saponins, which should be rinsed off before cooking.
Quinoa cooks in about 15 minutes and the seeds unwind into little tails when done.

items.title: Complete plant protein
items.content: Quinoa provides all essential amino acids, which is unusual for a plant food.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Quinoa contributes fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides magnesium, manganese, and folate
items.content: These nutrients support muscle function, metabolism, and cell function.

items.title: Provides iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immune function.

items.title: Naturally gluten-free
items.content: Quinoa suits people who avoid gluten, provided it is processed safely.

items.title: Saponins
items.content: The natural coating on quinoa tastes bitter and may irritate some people's stomachs, so rinse quinoa well before cooking.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Quinoa contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Allergic reactions and digestion
items.content: Quinoa allergy is uncommon but can occur, and large amounts of fiber may cause gas or bloating.

items.title: Gluten cross-contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose quinoa labeled gluten-free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse quinoa in a fine strainer and simmer it in about twice its volume of water until the seeds are tender, then fluff with a fork. Use it in salads, bowls, soups, stuffed vegetables, porridge, and patties, or as a rice substitute. Toasting the rinsed seeds briefly before cooking deepens the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry quinoa in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, where it keeps for a year or longer. Cooked quinoa should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days, or frozen.
